findings.description: No server_side_encryption_configuration block is defined, so objects in this bucket (which receives an uploaded vendor roster spreadsheet) are stored without enforced SSE-KMS or SSE-S3 encryption. Any data at rest is unprotected by a customer-controlled key and there is no key-policy layer of access control.

The bucket holding ledger exports declares no server_side_encryption_configuration, leaving financial export data stored without enforced encryption at rest, unlike the audit_trail bucket in the same file which uses aws:kms.

Versioning and access logging are configured, but no server_side_encryption_configuration is present, so model artifacts are stored unencrypted while their access logs are written to a KMS-encrypted bucket — the data is less protected than the log of access to it.

No server_side_encryption_configuration is defined. Operational runbooks commonly contain internal hostnames, escalation procedures, and recovery credentials or key locations, and are stored here without enforced encryption at rest.

No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block is associated with this bucket and, unlike the sibling buckets, it does not even declare acl = "private". It relies entirely on the account default, so any later ACL or policy change — or a permissive account-level default — could make the vendor roster and report data publicly readable.

No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block guards this bucket. The private ACL is the only control; without BlockPublicAcls/BlockPublicPolicy, a subsequent ACL grant or bucket policy could expose ledger exports publicly with no account-level backstop.
No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block is attached, so public ACLs or public bucket policies are not structurally blocked for this bucket.
No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block is attached, so public ACLs or public bucket policies are not structurally blocked for this bucket.

The audit log destination bucket has no aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block. Audit logs frequently reveal principal names, source IPs, and object keys; public exposure would leak reconnaissance data about the whole environment.
No bucket policy denies requests where aws:SecureTransport is false, so ledger export data may be read or written over unencrypted HTTP, permitting interception in transit.
No bucket policy enforces aws:SecureTransport, allowing plaintext HTTP access to report and vendor roster objects.
The audit log bucket has no policy requiring TLS, so log delivery and log retrieval may occur over unencrypted connections.

Versioning is not enabled, unlike the other buckets in this file. Without object versions, accidental or malicious overwrite and deletion of report data is unrecoverable, removing a key tamper-resistance control.
Versioning is disabled on the ledger export bucket, so overwritten or deleted financial records cannot be recovered and object tampering leaves no prior-version evidence.

force_destroy = true on the audit log bucket allows Terraform to delete the bucket and all retained audit logs without the object-emptying safeguard, enabling anti-forensic destruction of the evidence trail by anyone able to run an apply or destroy.
Unlike model_artifacts, this bucket sends no server access logs to audit_trail, so reads and writes of ledger export data leave no bucket-level access record for detection or forensic reconstruction.
No logging block directs access logs to the audit_trail bucket, so access to report and vendor roster objects is not recorded at the S3 bucket level.

A vendor roster spreadsheet is uploaded with no server_side_encryption or kms_key_id argument into aws_s3_bucket.reports_archive, which itself has no default encryption. Third-party vendor rosters typically contain contact and contractual PII and are stored here in cleartext.
